column4: The section contrasts a structure founded on taqwa with one that collapses into Hell; this verse identifies the opposing mosque built for harm, disbelief, and division, supplying the bad intention behind the unstable foundation in the next ayah.

The section sets the ravine-edge building against one founded on taqwa and seeking God's approval; this neighboring verse explicitly says the mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy, completing the positive side of the contrast.
The section's rejected hearer turns his back on the warning; this verse describes a man who turned away and became arrogant, the action immediately preceding his sentence to Saqar.
The section pairs denial and turning away with entry into the Fire; following the arrogant man's rejection, this verse says he will be made to enter Saqar, completing that warning scene.

The section sets the Lord who gives against Pharaoh's claim to be the highest ruler; this verse says sovereignty is God's to grant or take away, and honor or abase, exposing the king's claimed height as borrowed and temporary.

The section opens with night covering and day appearing, then speaks of the Lord who creates and gives; this verse joins night entering day with bringing life from death and providing without measure, meeting those images in one statement.
The section contrasts a king's temporary claim to elevation with God's lasting dominion; this verse says everyone on earth passes away, establishing what cannot remain.

The source section's wording وَجْهِ رَبِّهِ (92:20) makes the sought divine face central; this verse says the face of the Lord remains, joining that face to the passage's contrast between what passes and what endures.

The section says Musa's answer gathers creation, giving, and guidance; this continuation of the answer names the Lord who makes the earth a resting place, lays paths through it, sends water, and brings out plants, illustrating provision and direction.
The section's palace answer identifies the Lord as giver; this next verse tells people to eat and pasture their livestock from what God has provided, making the provision concrete.

The section's palace encounter contrasts God's guidance with denial and turning away; after Musa's answer, this verse says Pharaoh was shown every sign but denied them and refused, repeating the denial root ك ذ ب.

The section says no human favor can be repaid and worldly wealth will not save its owner; this verse calls people to spend before a Day with no bargaining, friendship, or intercession, directly joining giving to the limit of earthly ties.
The section's high garden yields double fruit after a downpour; this verse uses seed that multiplies manyfold as a likeness for spending in God's way, linking giving to fruitful increase.
The section describes wealth given for God's face; this verse says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves, clarifying the cost and quality of the open hand.

The section says wealth cannot help once its owner falls; this verse has the dying person ask for a brief delay so he can give charity and become righteous, showing the moment when withheld time and wealth can no longer be recovered.
The section places the failure of wealth at the moment of falling; this continuation says God does not delay a soul when its appointed time comes, completing the urgency of the preceding plea.
The section pairs night that covers with day that appears; this verse swears by the day as it displays, repeating the disclosure side of that image in a passage about the soul's moral outcome.

The section's opening night veils the course of human striving; this paired oath names the night as it covers (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا), repeating the concealment image before the passage turns to purification and failure.
